name: Hyprland
summary: A Wayland compositor and dynamic tiling window manager that owns protocol clients, monitor and surface resources, animated rendering, input routing, and a command-driven layout state.

features.name: Wayland compositor boundary
features.description: Hyprland implements the compositor side of the Wayland protocol, accepts client surfaces, and coordinates their scene placement, focus, rendering, and lifecycle through a single compositor process.
benefits: Keeps client protocol, policy, and presentation in one authoritative display server
Allows compositor policy to mediate surface focus, stacking, and output visibility
costs: A compositor fault can affect all managed clients
Protocol and policy changes must remain compatible with diverse Wayland clients

features.name: Dynamic tiling layout tree
features.description: Hyprland represents managed windows and groups in a mutable layout and workspace model; dispatchers and configuration commands change focus, movement, split orientation, grouping, and workspace placement.
benefits: Makes window placement and focus operations addressable as compositor state
Supports dynamic tiling alongside floating and grouped surfaces
costs: Mutable placement rules create ordering and edge cases during window lifecycle changes
Layout behavior depends on configuration and dispatcher semantics

features.name: Seat input and focus routing
features.description: Hyprland receives keyboard, pointer, and other libinput-backed events, applies device and binding configuration, and routes resulting actions or focus changes to the compositor's active surface and workspace state.
benefits: Centralizes device policy, keybind dispatch, and pointer/keyboard focus
Allows input actions to operate on the same layout state as protocol events
costs: Input behavior depends on device capabilities and configuration precedence
Incorrect focus or binding state can make windows appear unresponsive while the compositor remains alive

features.name: Output and render-resource model
features.description: Hyprland tracks monitors, workspaces, windows, surfaces, textures, and render damage as resources whose geometry and visibility determine frame composition for each output.
benefits: Separates output geometry and render resources from client application state
Enables per-monitor workspace placement and incremental scene updates
costs: Hotplug, scaling, damage, and animation add resource synchronization paths
GPU or output failures can invalidate resources independently of client protocol state

features.name: Animated lifecycle and failure boundary
features.description: Window, workspace, monitor, and animation state progresses through compositor-managed updates; failed client, protocol, output, or render operations are handled at different boundaries, so recovery may preserve compositor state while losing a surface or output.
benefits: Makes transient presentation state explicit rather than coupling it to client process state
Allows individual surfaces or outputs to be removed without treating every client event as a global restart
costs: Asynchronous animation and output transitions increase failure-path complexity
The fixed source does not establish transparent recovery for every GPU or protocol failure

mathematical_views.question: How do clients, protocol objects, surfaces, outputs, and compositor-owned render resources connect across a frame?
assumptions: Protocol objects and outputs are typed resource nodes
Rendering and GPU internals are abstracted as resource edges
The graph does not imply client access to another client's resources

mathematical_views.question: Which focus, split, workspace, group, and floating arrangements are reachable after compositor dispatchers and client lifecycle events?
assumptions: Windows and groups are nodes with geometry and focus metadata
Dispatchers and lifecycle callbacks are state transitions
The model abstracts animation interpolation and renderer timing

mathematical_views.question: What compositor state remains reachable when a client, surface, output, protocol request, or render resource fails?
assumptions: Client and output failures are distinct transitions
A removed surface may leave workspace and compositor state intact
The view is a candidate operational model, not a recovery guarantee

benefits: One policy boundary coordinates clients and presentation
costs: A process-wide fault threatens the display session

benefits: Tiling and focus are directly manipulable state
Input actions and layout commands share one policy model
costs: Device and binding configuration can create subtle routing failures

benefits: Per-output composition and damage are explicit
costs: Hotplug and GPU resource failures complicate consistency

benefits: Surface loss can be isolated from unrelated layout state
costs: Asynchronous transitions make failure diagnosis harder

relations.notes: The pinned compositor source creates a wl_display, adds a Wayland socket, and exports WAYLAND_DISPLAY; this is an implementation dependency on the Wayland server API.
